“Yes, that is easier said than done. At times one’s thoughts run so wild, or they come in tiny fragments and are so disconnected, or it is sheer madness that one sits there being driven round and round by; it is quite impossible to find words for it.”

He had put his arm around her waist and, with his other hand, bent her head in toward him so that it came to rest against his neck. They held each other in an embrace and sat for a while without speaking.

“But now I know what I am thinking about,” said Constance, pressing her lips against his beard.

“About what, then, Conny?”

“About what we have so often talked about, about how happy you have made me, about all our treasures, about everything we have lived through together, about the love you have brought forth in me by loving me, and especially about what you know, what lies ahead.”

“My beloved, my sweet one,” said Lorck, holding her closer to him. “How happy you make me—how blissful your words are, and how sweet your caresses. And you, who were so afraid to take me—” he added a little later, in a more tender voice.

“Not you any more than others—I felt reluctance or disgust, in general.”

“You wicked thing, who would have nothing to do with me. Do you remember how hard I had to strive? And if it had not been for the letter—ugh, I dare not think of it.”

“It was a dreadful time,” said Constance, “what a creature I had become. That you really had the courage to take me on was well done of you”—she clung to him.

“I loved you, Conny.”

“And at the beginning, when we were married—do you remember how foolish I was—utterly miserable from shyness?”

“Fundamentally, I have been quite persistent, Conny; you must admit that, for you did everything to discourage me, but, as I said, I loved you—I had never loved before I began to love you.”

“Is it really true, Nils—tell me, is it true?”

“Yes, my dear, I know that now. If it had not been for you, I would never have learned to know love. And now, when we have our treasure to look forward to—I am supremely happy, Conny—”

“But you have been in love with others, surely—yes, and been involved with others?”

“That was nonsense and foolishness, Conny; only you have made life alive for me.”

“And it is the same for you too, Conny,” he continued a little later; “your life begins only with me, does it not?”

She did not answer.

“For you love me; say that you love me.”

“You know that, Nils,” she said softly.

“But say it all the same—it is so sweet to hear.”

A strange sensation came over her. She felt an urge to shake his arms off and run away. It was as though something ghostly in the darkness were creeping up behind her, something she did not dare turn around to look at. It made her shudder. And then, at that same moment, she remembered the gentle pleasure that had slipped over her when Mejer, quite by chance today, had come to rest his arm on the back of the chair in which she was sitting. But now she wanted to get away from all this, and with a leap she entered the circle of thoughts of love and happiness in which she had lived during these many months. She wrapped the memories of the sweet hours and all the enchanting little things that had passed between her and Lorck around herself like a shield. She wanted to be happy; she was happy.

“I love you,” she said, “love, love you,” and her kisses and caresses were more ardent than ever before.

Lorck pressed her to his heart, an enraptured smile upon his half-open lips. She buried her face in his soft, thick beard.

“But what is this?” he said with a sudden jerk. “I am becoming ill.” He clutched her hand and bent forward, groaning. Violent chills passed through him.

“You have caught cold from that ice cream,” said Constance. “Come, let us go upstairs.”

With difficulty he rose and, supported by Constance’s arm, walked up through the garden and into the hotel; from time to time he stopped and groaned with pain.

When they had reached their rooms, Constance was alarmed by his pallor; a cold sweat lay upon his brow, and he complained of unbearable nausea. She immediately sent for a doctor.

He was a somewhat elderly, stocky little Frenchman with masses of gray hair and beard. He told Constance that her husband had caught a severe cold, but that he hoped it would not become serious. Then he promised to send some medicine and to return the next morning.

XXV.

Lorck was laid up with gastric fever. Constance nursed him with untiring care. Most of the time he did not recognize her, but took her for someone else; he frequently called her Kristine.

The doctor obtained a deaconess who was to keep watch every other night, alternating with Constance. He thought that three or four weeks would pass before they could even consider the journey home; apart from that, there was no danger, provided only that they observed due caution.

Mejer had now given up traveling and told Constance that he would remain as long as he could be of use to her. Constance had thanked him with great warmth and had made no secret of how glad she was about his decision.

878

He was a daily help and encouragement to her, fetched the medicine from the pharmacy, and was constantly at hand to perform small services for her. Every day he brought her flowers or fruit and induced her to take a little fresh air in the garden. Sometimes he came upstairs four times to suggest that she take a walk, and only the fifth time was it convenient, for she would not go unless Lorck was asleep. Then a maid would come and keep watch in the adjoining room, with orders to fetch the lady immediately if the gentleman awoke.

When Lorck was lucid, Mejer went in from time to time and asked how he was doing. Lorck nodded with a faint smile and always said that he was better now. Sometimes he asked for the newspapers, and Mejer would then tell him one thing or another. When he began to recover, Mejer read to him until he fell asleep or said that he was tired.

Once he had thanked Mejer for his great kindness toward him and Constance and said that it was a comfort to him to know that Constance had him to turn to.

About a fortnight after Lorck had fallen ill, Constance was sitting with him in the large armchair at the head of the bed. He had been restless all morning and delirious for a moment now and then. The doctor had given him some calming medicine, and in the course of the afternoon he had fallen into a slumber. Constance had then taken her customary walk in the garden and had found Lorck asleep upon her return. Now she had sunk back with fatigue. The book she had been reading lay in her lap; her fingers had released their hold on it and rested quietly beside it. She awoke at the sound of someone walking in the other room, straightened up, and peered through the half-open door. It was the maid with the mail. She motioned to her to put it down on the table and then settled back to doze again.
